lead: Speech and data sit near 0 Hz, so a wire or antenna will not carry them far. Modulation lifts the message onto a high-frequency sine carrier by varying its amplitude, frequency or phase. The same three knobs carry bits, giving ASK, FSK and PSK. This chapter covers AM, FM and PM, then the digital forms up to QAM, where baud rate and bit rate differ.
prereq: You need 2.1 for amplitude, frequency and phase, 2.3 for bandwidth and capacity, and 2.4 for band-pass media.

sections.h3: Why a signal needs a carrier

blocks.text: A baseband signal — voice or bits — holds most energy near 0 Hz. Many media do not pass 0 Hz. A radio channel, cable TV plant or telephone line with a transformer passes only a band around a centre frequency. That is a band-pass channel. Baseband pushed into it gives nothing useful out.

Modulation fixes this. The carrier is the sine wave A<sub>c</sub> cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t), where A<sub>c</sub> is carrier peak amplitude in volts, f<sub>c</sub> carrier frequency in hertz, and t time in seconds. Vary one carrier parameter in step with the message. The message now rides inside the channel band.

The antenna is a second reason. An antenna radiates well near a quarter wavelength, λ/4, with λ = c/f and c = 3 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s. A 1 kHz tone has λ = 300 km, so λ/4 = 75 km — useless. At 100 MHz, λ = 3 m and λ/4 = 75 cm. Higher frequency makes radiation practical.
Third, many signals can share one medium on different carriers. That is frequency-division multiplexing (FDM); 2.7 builds on it.
In AM the carrier amplitude follows the message. For one tone:

blocks.where: A<sub>c</sub> is carrier peak amplitude in V, f<sub>c</sub> carrier frequency in Hz, f<sub>m</sub> message frequency in Hz, t time in s, and μ = A<sub>m</sub>/A<sub>c</sub> the modulation index (no units), with A<sub>m</sub> message peak amplitude in V.

blocks.text: The square bracket is the envelope. It swings between A<sub>c</sub>(1 + μ) and A<sub>c</sub>(1 − μ). Multiplying the cosines gives the carrier f<sub>c</sub> and two sidebands at f<sub>c</sub> − f<sub>m</sub> and f<sub>c</sub> + f<sub>m</sub>. One tone occupies 2f<sub>m</sub> Hz. A message band reaching f<sub>m(max)</sub> takes 2f<sub>m(max)</sub> Hz.

Keep μ ≤ 1. At μ = 1 the envelope just touches zero. Past that — overmodulation — the envelope crosses over, phase flips for part of each cycle, and recovered audio inverts and distorts. More depth is not more loudness; it is a broken signal.

The carrier alone carries no information. DSB-SC (double-sideband suppressed carrier) removes it to save power. SSB-SC (single-sideband suppressed carrier) also removes one sideband, halving bandwidth to f<sub>m</sub>; shortwave radio uses it.

In FM the instantaneous frequency is f<sub>c</sub> + k<sub>f</sub>m(t), where k<sub>f</sub> is frequency sensitivity in Hz/V and m(t) the message in volts. For a tone of peak amplitude A<sub>m</sub>, peak frequency deviation is Δf = k<sub>f</sub>A<sub>m</sub> Hz. The FM modulation index is β = Δf/f<sub>m</sub>, a pure number.

blocks.where: B is practical FM bandwidth in Hz, Δf peak frequency deviation in Hz, and f<sub>m</sub> the highest message frequency in Hz (Carson's rule).

blocks.text: In PM the phase shifts in proportion to m(t); the index is peak phase deviation in radians. FM and PM waves have a constant envelope, so a limiter strips amplitude noise before detection — that is their noise immunity. The price is bandwidth: with β = 5, Carson gives B ≈ 12f<sub>m</sub>.

sections.h3: Digital modulation: ASK, FSK, PSK, QAM

blocks.text: Digital modulation uses the same three knobs, driven by bits.

ASK switches carrier amplitude between levels. When one level is zero it is on-off keying (OOK). Noise adds to amplitude, so ASK is fragile but cheap. A light source switched fully on and off is an ASK signal, which suits optical fibre.
FSK jumps the carrier between two frequencies (BFSK). The envelope stays constant, so clipping and amplitude distortion do not matter; bandwidth is wider than ASK.

PSK switches phase. BPSK uses two phases 180° apart, giving 1 bit per symbol. These symbols are as far apart as two points on a circle can be, so noise must be large to cause an error; of ASK, FSK and PSK, BPSK gives the fewest bit errors at the same signal-to-noise ratio. QPSK uses four phases 90° apart, giving 2 bits per symbol in the same bandwidth.

QAM varies amplitude and phase together, placing M points in a constellation — a plot of the two carrier components. QAM-16 is a 4 × 4 grid with 4 bits per symbol; QAM-64 is an 8 × 8 grid with 6 bits per symbol. More points mean closer neighbours, so higher QAM needs a cleaner channel (see 2.2).

blocks.where: R<sub>b</sub> is bit rate in bit/s, R<sub>s</sub> symbol (baud) rate in symbols/s, and M the number of constellation states.

blocks.text: The modem does this at both ends: modulator on send, demodulator on receive.

figure.caption: One full cycle of the 1 kHz message: the AM envelope has a 100 kHz carrier under it, and its edges swing between 16 V and 4 V. With modulation index 0.6 the envelope never reaches zero, so the recovered audio stays clean.

examples.question: A 1 kHz tone with peak amplitude 6 V amplitude-modulates a 100 kHz carrier of peak amplitude 10 V. Find μ, sidebands, bandwidth and peak amplitude. A QAM-16 modem runs at 2400 baud; find its bit rate.
steps: Data: f<sub>m</sub> = 1 kHz, A<sub>m</sub> = 6 V, f<sub>c</sub> = 100 kHz, A<sub>c</sub> = 10 V.
μ = A<sub>m</sub>/A<sub>c</sub> = 6 ÷ 10 = 0.6, so 60% and no overmodulation.
Peak amplitude: A<sub>c</sub>(1 + μ) = 10 × 1.6 = 16 V; minimum = 10 × 0.4 = 4 V.
QAM-16 carries log₂16 = 4 bits per symbol.
examples.answer: μ = 0.6 (60%) with no overmodulation, sidebands at 99 kHz and 101 kHz, bandwidth 2 kHz, peak amplitude 16 V (minimum 4 V), and the QAM-16 modem delivers 4 bits per symbol at 9600 bit/s.
examples.check:
import math
Am = 6.0
Ac = 10.0
fm = 1e3
fc = 100e3
mu = Am/Ac
print(mu)
print((fc-fm)/1e3)
print((fc+fm)/1e3)
print(2*fm/1e3)
print(Ac*(1+mu))
print(Ac*(1-mu))
M = 16
bps = math.log2(M)
print(bps)
print(2400*bps)

examples.question: A QAM-64 modem runs at 2000 baud over a clean link. Find its bit rate.
examples.answer: The bit rate is 12000 bit/s, i.e. 12 kbit/s.
examples.check:
import math
Rs = 2000
M = 64
bps = math.log2(M)
print(bps)
print(Rs*bps)

traps: μ > 1 is not deeper modulation. Past 100% the envelope crosses over and audio inverts and distorts.
Bit rate is baud rate × log₂M, not baud rate × M. QAM-16 at 2400 baud is 9600 bit/s, not 38400 bit/s.
A single-tone AM wave has bandwidth 2f<sub>m</sub>, not f<sub>m</sub>. The f<sub>m</sub> figure belongs to single sideband.
In FM, Δf is peak frequency deviation, not bandwidth. Carson's rule adds Δf and f<sub>m</sub> before doubling.
Do not swap f<sub>c</sub> and f<sub>m</sub>: sidebands are f<sub>c</sub> ± f<sub>m</sub>, so the carrier is the larger number in an AM radio link.

quiz.q: Define the AM modulation index and state the condition for no overmodulation.
quiz.a: μ = A<sub>m</sub>/A<sub>c</sub>, message peak amplitude divided by carrier peak amplitude. No overmodulation when μ ≤ 1.

quiz.q: Why does the carrier of an AM wave carry no information?
quiz.a: It is a fixed sine at f<sub>c</sub> with constant amplitude; all message-dependent variation is in the two sidebands. Removing it — DSB-SC — leaves the message recoverable.

quiz.q: Why does FM resist noise better than AM, and what does it pay?
quiz.a: FM keeps a constant envelope, so a limiter removes amplitude noise before detection. It pays in bandwidth: Carson gives B ≈ 2(Δf + f<sub>m</sub>), many times the message bandwidth.

quiz.q: A 2 kHz tone with peak amplitude 4 V modulates a 200 kHz carrier of peak amplitude 8 V. Find μ, sidebands, bandwidth and peak amplitude.
quiz.a: μ = 4 ÷ 8 = 0.5. Sidebands at 198 kHz and 202 kHz. Bandwidth = 4 kHz = 2f<sub>m</sub>. Peak amplitude = 8 × 1.5 = 12 V.

quiz.q: A QAM-16 modem transmits 3000 symbols per second. Find its bit rate.
quiz.a: log₂16 = 4 bits per symbol, so bit rate = 3000 × 4 = 12000 bit/s.

quiz.q: An operator drives an AM transmitter to μ = 1.4 to get more power across. Explain what a listener hears.
quiz.a: The envelope passes through zero and crosses over for part of each cycle, so phase inverts. The envelope detector folds the waveform and recovered audio distorts and partly inverts. Overmodulation causes splatter into neighbouring channels, not more loudness.

quiz.q: Why does QAM-64 need a cleaner channel than QAM-16 at the same peak amplitude?
quiz.a: QAM-64 puts 64 points into the same peak swing, so neighbours are closer than in the 16-point grid. The same noise voltage is more likely to cross a decision boundary, so a higher signal-to-noise ratio is needed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Wi-Fi uses QAM-64 up to QAM-1024 with OFDM, and LTE goes to 256-QAM. Error-vector magnitude (EVM) measures how far received symbols sit from ideal points. Software-defined radios change scheme in code. Search constellation diagram, EVM and peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR).
